In SORESPO, all three device types are pruned this way, each with a list of the YANG paths to retain. spec/src/sorespo_gen.act

# Keep only the XR nodes that sorespo actively uses.
xr_paths = [
"/um-hostname-cfg:hostname",
"/um-hostname-cfg:hostname/system-network-name",
"/um-interface-cfg:interfaces",
"/um-interface-cfg:interfaces/interface",
"/um-interface-cfg:interfaces/interface/interface-name",
"/um-interface-cfg:interfaces/interface/description",
"/um-interface-cfg:interfaces/interface/shutdown",
...

Compiler performance improvements

The platform core developers are actively working on improving the performance of the YANG transpilation and compilation process. We are combining several strategies to achieve this, including generating total types during the YANG to Acton transpilation, improving the efficiency of the Acton compiler, and support for shipping binary type libraries that can be imported directly without needing to compile the device types locally.

The goal of these improvements is to allow for the use of full device models without pruning, while still maintaining a fast development workflow.

items.title: Defining transforms
items.text:
For a StratoWeave system to store and act on data at each layer, the system specification must include transform definitions. Create a transform by annotating a list or container in any transform layer's YANG with the sw:transform statement from the StratoWeave YANG extensions.

spec/yang/cfs/netinfra.yang
...
container netinfra {
  description "Network infrastructure";
  list router {
    description "Network Infrastructure Router";
    key name;

    sw:transform sorespo.cfs.Router;
    tmf:cfs-service "Router";

    leaf name {
      type string;
    }
...

The value of the sw:transform annotation should be the import path to a class containing a transform() method. See the transforms section for more details on how to write the transform logic.

items.title: Defining RFS transforms
items.text:
The lowest transform layer in the system is the RFS layer, StratoWeave expects this layer to be modeled according to the RFS YANG schema shippped with the platform. Augment the sw-rfs:rfs list from that schema to define the RFS layer transforms for your system. The RFS transforms also use a special annotation, sw:rfs-transform, which is a variant of sw:transform that supplies the transform with device information together with the input data.

spec/yang/rfs/sorespo-rfs.yang
module sorespo-rfs {
...
  augment "/sw-rfs:rfs" {
    container base-config {
     sw:rfs-transform sorespo.rfs.BaseConfig;

    leaf role {
      type string;
    }
...

items.title: Using YANG augmentation
items.text:
StratoWeave also supports using YANG augmentations to define transforms on schema nodes that are defined in other modules. This is especially useful for applying transforms to standard models that you do not want to edit directly, such as published IETF modules.

spec/yang/cfs/sorespo-ietf-l3vpn-svc.yang
...
augment "/l3vpn-svc:l3vpn-svc/l3vpn-svc:vpn-services/l3vpn-svc:vpn-service" {
  sw:transform sorespo.cfs.L3VpnVpnService;
  tmf:cfs-service "L3VPN VPN Service";
}
...

The added benefit of using YANG augmentation for transform definitions on the YANG modules in the CFS layer is that it allows you to keep the original YANG module clean of any StratoWeave-specific annotations. This can be desirable when a northbound NETCONF client downloads the YANG schemas from the system.

The StratoWeave northbound NETCONF interface is not yet available.

items.title: Defining TMF Service/Resource mappings
items.text:
StratoWeave implements the YANG to TM Forum mapping defined in draft-lambrechts-onsen-yang-tmf-mapping-00. To annotate your YANG models with TMF mapping instructions, import the ietf-yang-tmf-map module from the StratoWeave YANG extensions and use the tmf:cfs-service annotation to indicate which CFS service each YANG node corresponds to.

spec/yang/cfs/netinfra.yang
...
container netinfra {
  description "Network infrastructure";
  list router {
    description "Network Infrastructure Router";
    key name;

    sw:transform sorespo.cfs.Router;
    tmf:cfs-service "Router";

    leaf name {
      type string;
    }
...

items.title: Generating the system specification
items.text:
Whenever you have modified the system specification definition, either by changing the YANG models or the generator logic, execute the make gen command to re-generate sysspec.atd, the layer modules, and device types. 

make gen

How system spec generation works

The gen Make target first builds the spec/src/sorespo_gen.act Acton program, then runs the resulting binary. 

cd spec && acton build $(DEP_OVERRIDES) && out/bin/sorespo_gen

items.title: Testing
items.text:
StratoWeave projects use the standard Acton testing model described in Testing and Snapshot testing. Acton discovers test cases whose names start with _test_, supports both synchronous and asynchronous test harnesses, and compares returned strings or t.success(...) values against files in snapshots/expected/....

Regular Acton unit tests work well for testing StratoWeave transforms and helper functions. Build end-to-end tests with stratoweave.test_main(...) and stratoweave.testing.TestRig to apply Layer 0 input, inspect layer state, and snapshot rendered device configuration with device_adata_snapshot().

The repository Makefile is the canonical entry point:

make test

That target runs:

acton test $(DEP_OVERRIDES)

items.title: Test scopes
items.text: StratoWeave deployments usually benefit from three test scopes.

items.title: Focused transform tests
items.text:
For a regular transform, instantiate the class directly and exercise it with typed inputs or XML. A focused transform test is usually the cheapest way to verify one abstraction step in isolation.

def _test_inter_router():
    xmlin = """<router>
    <name>rtr1</name>
    <asn>65001</asn>
    </router>"""
    transform = dummy.inter.Router()
    out, _ = transform.transform_xml(xml.decode(xmlin), yang.gdata.Container())
    return out.to_xmlstr()

Use this style when the main question is: given this input, did the transform produce the right next-layer data?

items.title: Device-aware RFS tests
items.text:
RFS transforms usually depend on device capabilities, so the test often constructs a mock DeviceInfo and then calls the transform directly. This keeps the test fast while still checking vendor selection and device-specific rendering logic.

proc def _test_rfs_interface_junos(t: testing.SyncT):
    modeled_input = dummy.rfs.Interface.input_type()(...) 
    mock_di = stratoweave.ttt.DeviceInfo("edge-1", {...})
    transform = dummy.rfs.Interface(t.log_handler)
    out = transform.transform(modeled_input, mock_di).to_gdata()
    return out.to_xmlstr()

Use this when the behavior depends on vendor modules, device naming, supported features, or other RFS context.

items.title: End-to-end system tests
items.text:
For full pipeline validation, build layer-0 input data and run it through the real SYSSPEC. stratoweave.test_main(...) creates a TestRig that can apply input config, inspect layer state, and capture rendered device configurations as a snapshot string.

actor _test_service_snapshot(t: testing.AsyncT):
    root = sample.layers.y_0.root()
    root.netinfra.router.create("rtr1", 1, "ietf")

    tr = stratoweave.test_main(sample.sysspec.SYSSPEC, t.log_handler)

    def cont(_r: value):
        t.success(tr.device_adata_snapshot())

    tr.edit_config(root.to_gdata(), cont)

The local minisys/src/test_mini.act suite shows three useful system-wide patterns:

  • _test_netinfra1(t: testing.AsyncT): apply a small but complete baseline config and snapshot the rendered device output. This is the most direct end-to-end check for whether a service model produces the expected device configuration.
  • _test_netinfra_router_oper(t: testing.AsyncT): apply config, then poll the CFS view until a transform actor or RFS stage publishes operational state. This is the right pattern when the system under test updates config false state asynchronously and the test needs a bounded timeout.
  • _test_l3vpn1(t: testing.AsyncT): model a service that spans multiple routers and endpoints, then snapshot the final rendered output for all affected devices. This is useful when validating decomposition across services, intermediate layers, and per-device config generation.

Use end-to-end tests when a change crosses layers or when a regression would only be visible after the whole system has processed the input.

items.title: Recommended workflow
items.text:
1. Update the YANG spec or transform implementation.
  2. Run make gen if the change touched spec/yang, generated layers, or the system layout.
  3. Add or update the closest _test_* case.
  4. Run make test.
  5. If a snapshot changed intentionally, inspect snapshots/output/... versus snapshots/expected/..., then accept it with acton test --accept.

items.title: Transforms
items.text: The definition of a transform is done in the system specification through the StratoWeave sw:transform and sw:rfs-transform YANG extensions. Once the system specification includes the necessary transform definitions, it is up to a service developer to implement the transform() method and/or Transform Actor.

items.title: The transform function
items.text:
Each transform is implemented as a class that inherits from a generated base class and implements a transform() function which is a pure function that takes input data and returns output data.

  • The input data is typed according to YANG schema for the node (i.e., the list element or container) on which the transform is defined.
  • The output data should be typed according to the YANG schema for the next layer's input.

The transform() function cannot have side effects, access other system information, subscribe to any data or persist state. If you need to do any of those things, you should implement a Transform Actor instead, which can manage subscriptions and maintain state. See the Transform Actor section for more details on that pattern.

The transform function should always produce the same output for a given input. You should not perform any non-deterministic operations such as generating random numbers or allocating new IDs in the transform function.

Because the transform() function is a pure function, the StratoWeave transaction engine can call it at any time, e.g. when the input data changes or when the system is restarted and needs to recompute the desired device configuration.

In its simplest form, the transform() function can just return an empty output object: 

class Router(base.Router):
    def transform(self, i):
        o = base.o_root()

        return o

No-op transform functions

The only way for a StratoWeave system to persist input (e.g. configuration) received on its northbound interfaces is to write it to a part of the YANG schema that is located inside of a transform. If you want to persist some input data but not use it (yet), a no-op transform function that returns an empty output root object is a valid way to do that.

items.title: Accessing transform function input
items.text:
The input data is available as the first argument to the transform() method, usually named i. The input is typed according to the YANG schema for the node on which the transform is defined.

Consider this YANG snippet:

spec/yang/cfs/fridge.yang
list fridge {
  key name;

  sw:transform dummy.foo.Fridge;

  leaf name {
    type string;
  }
  leaf manufacturer {
    type enum {
      enum "Fridgetech";
      enum "FrostCorp";
      enum "ChillMasters";
      enum "IceBox Inc.";
    }
  }
  list shelf {
    key id;
    leaf id {
      type uint32;
    }
    leaf capacity {
      type uint32;
      mandatory true;
    }
  }

In the transform() function, the input i will provide access to the name, manufacturer, and shelf nodes according to that schema: src/dummy/foo.act

class Fridge(base.Fridge):
    def transform(self, i):
        o = base.o_root()

        print(i.name.upper())
        manufacturer = i.manufacturer
        if manufacturer is not None:
            print(manufacturer.upper())
        for shelf in i.shelf:
            print("Shelf {shelf.id} has capacity {shelf.capacity}")

        return o

Accessing optional input

In this example, the manufacturer leaf is optional, in many cases you must perform a is not None check before using it. See the optional types section for more details on how to work with optional input data.

items.title: Writing transform output
items.text:
The output data should be typed according to the YANG schema for the next layer's input. The output is constructed by starting with a call to base.o_root() to get an empty output object and then populating it with data from the input or derived values.

If the next layer's YANG schema also has a list of fridges and we wanted to simply copy the input fridge to an output fridge with some minor modifications, the transform function might look like this: src/dummy/foo.act

class Fridge(base.Fridge):
    def transform(self, i):
        o = base.o_root()
        fridge = o.fridge.create(
            i.name.upper(),  # use the same name but uppercase it
            manufacturer=i.manufacturer,
        )
        for shelf in i.shelf:
            fridge.shelf.create(
                shelf.id + 500,  # assign new id to shelf
                capacity=shelf.capacity,
            )
        return o

items.title: The RFS transform function
items.text:
The RFS layer in a StratoWeave system has a specific pattern, as outlined in the system specification documentation.

The input data i is still typed according to the YANG schema for the node on which the transform is defined, but the transform can also use the di argument to access information about the device such as its capabilities, modules, and other metadata. src/sorespo/rfs.act

class IbgpNeighbor(base.IbgpNeighbor):
    def transform_function(self, i, di):
        if "Cisco-IOS-XR-um-hostname-cfg" in di.modules:
            dev = xr25.root()
            bgp_as = dev.um_router_bgp_cfg_router.bgp.as_.create(i.asn)
            nb = bgp_as.neighbors.neighbor.create(i.address, description=i.description)
            nb.use.neighbor_group = "IPV4-IBGP"
            return dev
        elif "http://xml.juniper.net/netconf/junos/1.0" in di.modules or "junos-conf-root" in di.modules:
            dev = crpd24.root()
            bgp = dev.configuration.protocols.bgp
            g = bgp.group.create("IPV4-IBGP")
            g.neighbor.create(i.address, description=i.description)
            return dev

        raise UnsupportedDevice()

items.title: The Transform Actor
items.text:
When your use case requires side effects, subscriptions, or access to other system information, you can implement a Transform Actor in combination with a transform() method.

We distinguish between some common "use cases" for Transform Actors:

  • Multi-stage transforms: not all device operations can be completed in a single NETCONF configuration transaction. For example, it may be necessary to first create some basic system information such as a hostname, then execute an RPC to generate a certificate signing request, and then write the resulting certificate back to the device.
  • Reactive transforms: some transform logic needs to react to changes in device information such as operational state or inventory. For example, if a linecard is inserted into a device, the system may need to automatically create some operating mode configuration for that linecard.
  • State publishing: A transform can expose state information, modeled as config False in YANG. The Transform Actor can populate that state information based on operational data it has received from device state or the state of other transforms it has subscribed to or any other information it has access to.

These use cases are not mutually exclusive, and a single Transform Actor may need to do all of these things at once or more.

items.title: Project setup
items.text:
To create a new StratoWeave project, we recommend you clone SORESPO. The SOmewhat REalistic Service Provider Orchestrator is a sample project that we maintain to demonstrate best practices for structuring StratoWeave projects.

Set up project
git clone https://github.com/stratoweave/sorespo.git

Warning

You do NOT need to clone the StratoWeave framework itself. All SORESPO dependencies will be downloaded by the Acton package manager at build time.

items.title: Development Environment
items.text:
StratoWeave is written in the Acton Programming Language, so you will need to set up an Acton development environment to work with it. Use the Acton APT repository on Debian or Ubuntu, or Homebrew on macOS.

Debian / Ubuntu
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo wget -q -O /etc/apt/keyrings/acton.asc https://apt.acton-lang.io/acton.gpg
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/acton.asc
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/acton.asc] http://apt.acton-lang.io/ stable main" | sudo tee -a /etc/apt/sources.list.d/acton.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -qy acton
macOS
brew install actonlang/acton/acton

items.title: Project Structure
items.text:
StratoWeave projects have a specific directory structure that organizes the various components of the project. Here is an overview of the typical project with files that you will be interested in modifying as you develop your system specification and transform code. Project structure

├── spec
│   ├── src
│   │   └── sorespo_gen.act
│   └── yang
│       ├── cfs
│       │   ├── ietf-l3vpn-svc.yang
│       │   ├── ietf-yang-types.yang
│       │   ├── netinfra.yang
│       │   └── sorespo-ietf-l3vpn-svc.yang
│       ├── inter
│       │   ├── l3pvn-inter.yang
│       │   └── netinfra-inter.yang
│       ├── rfs
│       │   └── sorespo-rfs.yang
│       ├── CiscoIosXr_25_3_1
│       │   └── ... (Cisco IOS-XR Device Adapter YANG models)
│       ├── JuniperCRPD_24_4R1_9
│       │   └── ... (Juniper cRPD Device Adapter YANG models)
│       └── NokiaSRLinux_25_3_2
│           └── ... (Nokia SR Linux Device Adapter YANG models)
└── src
    ├── sorespo
    │   ├── cfs.act
    │   ├── inter.act
    │   ├── rfs.act
    │   ├── device_types.act
    │   ├── devices
    │   │   └── ... (Auto-generated device definitions based on YANG models)
    │   ├── layers
    │   │   └── ... (Auto-generated layer definitions based on YANG models)
    │   └── sysspec.act
    └── sorespo.act

A quick overview of the most important files:

  • spec/src/sorespo_gen.act This is the main entry point for generating the system specification. Here you define the layers of your system and how they are composed together. You also specify which YANG models to use for each layer.
  • spec/yang/ - This directory contains the YANG models that make up the system specification.
    • cfs/, inter/, and rfs/ contain the service models for the 3 transform layers in SORESPO, e.g. Customer-facing, Resource-facing, and an intermediate layer.
    • CiscoIosXr_25_3_1/, JuniperCRPD_24_4R1_9/, and NokiaSRLinux_25_3_2/ contain the vendor YANG for the relevant device adapters.
  • src/sorespo/ - This directory contains all the Acton code from which the orchestrator is built.
    • cfs.act, inter.act, and rfs.act contain the transform code for the 3 transform layers in SORESPO.

items.title: Development Workflow
items.text:
There are two distinct phases in the StratoWeave development workflow, the first involves modifications to the System Specification, and the second resolves primarily around modifications to the Transform Code.

graph LR
  A[Start] --> B{System Specification Modifications?};
  B -->|Yes| C[Regenerate Project];
  B -->|No| D{Transform Code Modifications?};
  D ---->|Yes| E[Build Project];
  C --> E;
  D ---->|No| F[Done!];
  E --> F;

After modifying the system specification, e.g. any YANG models, you will need to (re)generate the project. (Re)generate project

make gen

After modifying the system specification and/or the transform code, you will need to (re)build the project 1. (Re)build project

make build

The generated orchestrator binary will be located at out/bin/sorespo.

You can also execute the included test suite to verify that everything is working correctly. Run tests

make test

  1. It is also possible to cross-compile for other platforms. This can be very useful when developing e.g. on macOS but deploying to Linux-based containers or servers. Cross-compilation make targets

    make build-linux-x86_64
make build-linux-aarch64
make build-macos-aarch64
    ↩

items.title: Operations Guide
items.text: This section of the documentation is for operators responsible for deploying and maintaining StratoWeave-based systems.

items.title: Device management
items.text: StratoWeave keeps managed devices in the intent tree rather than in a separate out-of-band inventory. The transform layer immediately above the RFS layer owns that intent: it decides which devices exist, which generated device type each device uses, how the orchestrator reaches it, and which RFS transforms should be created for it.

items.title: Build-time: device adapters come from the system spec
items.text:
Each supported vendor OS version is declared as a separate device type in the system specification. Every DeviceType.from_dir(...) call loads one specific directory of YANG modules, and the generated application builds a typed device adapter for that exact module set.

spec/src/sorespo_gen.act
spec = stratoweave.build.SysSpec("sorespo", [
        cfs_layer,
        rfs_layer,
], [
        stratoweave.build.DeviceType.from_dir(fc, "CiscoIosXr_25_3_1", "yang/CiscoIosXr_25_3_1"),
        stratoweave.build.DeviceType.from_dir(fc, "CiscoIosXr_25_4_1", "yang/CiscoIosXr_25_4_1"),
        stratoweave.build.DeviceType.from_dir(fc, "JuniperCRPD_24_4R1_9", "yang/JuniperCRPD_24_4R1_9"),
])

spec.gen_app(fc, "../src/")

When a vendor ships a new release with a different set of YANG modules or revisions, add a new directory and a new DeviceType.from_dir(...) entry, and rebuild the application. At runtime, the value written into device.type must match one of these device type names exactly.

items.title: Operations-time: device entries are part of intent
items.text:
Operators do not create DeviceMgr instances directly. Instead, they submit northbound intent, and the layer above RFS emits two related outputs for each managed device:

  • a device entry that selects the generated adapter and supplies connection details
  • an rfs entry that carries the resource-facing service data for that same device

In a two-layer system this is the CFS transform. In a three-layer system it would be the intermediate layer.

items.title: Exposing device inputs on the northbound
items.text:
If device address, credentials, or adapter selection should be operator provided, those inputs must exist in the northbound YANG model.

spec/yang/cfs/netinfra.yang
...
    container netinfra {
        list router {
            key name;

            sw:transform sorespo.cfs.Router;

            leaf name {
                type string;
            }
            leaf device-type {
                type string;
            }
            leaf mgmt-address {
                type inet:host;
            }
            leaf device-username {
                type string;
            }
            leaf device-password {
                type string;
            }
        }
    }

If your northbound model exposes these leaves, operators can provide them in a startup XML file or over a northbound API such as NETCONF:

SORESPO-style northbound intent
<netinfra xmlns="...">
    <router>
        <name>pe1</name>
        <device-type>CiscoIosXr_25_3_1</device-type>
        <mgmt-address>192.0.2.10</mgmt-address>
        <device-username>netops</device-username>
        <device-password>netops-password</device-password>
    </router>
</netinfra>

In other scenarios, the northbound model may not expose these leaves, and the transform layer above RFS may instead look up the device type and credentials from an internal database or a secrets manager. In that case, the northbound intent would only need to provide e.g. the device name, and the transform would fill in the rest.

items.title: Creating device and RFS entries in the transform
items.text:
The transform above RFS creates the device entry and the matching RFS subtree together. The important pattern is:

src/sorespo/cfs.act
class Router(base.Router):
        def transform(self, i, linked, dynstate):
                o = base.o_root()

                dev = o.device.create(i.name)
                dev.type = i.device_type

                oob = dev.address.create("oob")
                oob.address = i.mgmt_address

                dev.credentials.username = i.device_username
                dev.credentials.password = i.device_password

                rfs = o.rfs.create(i.name)
                rfs.base_config.name = i.name

                return o

Here, o.device.create(i.name) adds the managed device entry consumed by the generated device layer. dev.type selects one of the build-time device types, for example CiscoIosXr_25_3_1. o.rfs.create(i.name) creates the RFS object bound to that same device.

If credentials should not be operator supplied, keep them out of the northbound YANG and set the same dev.credentials fields from an internal lookup instead.

items.title: SSH transport parameters
items.text:
Every SSH-based adapter -- NETCONF over SSH and the IOS XE CLI adapter -- reads its transport settings from the device's ssh container, or from the ssh container of its extra-adapter entry. Leave it out and the SSH library's defaults apply; set it to deal with devices that need something narrower or older.

To expose these settings in another model, import stratoweave-ssh and use its ssh-client-config grouping inside an ssh container:

import stratoweave-ssh {
  prefix sw-ssh;
}

container ssh {
  uses sw-ssh:ssh-client-config;
}

Include swyang.ssh in the layer's models when generating the application, and copy the settings to dev.ssh in its transform.

src/sorespo/cfs.act
dev.ssh.cipher = ["aes128-ctr"]
dev.ssh.key_exchange = ["diffie-hellman-group14-sha256"]
dev.ssh.host_key_algorithm = ["ssh-rsa"]
dev.ssh.minimum_rsa_bits = u64(1024)

The algorithm leaf-lists (cipher, mac, key-exchange, host-key-algorithm, public-key-algorithm, compression-algorithm) are ordered preference lists, most preferred first, and an empty one means "use the library default". host-key-algorithm is what decides which host key type the device presents. The remaining leaves are compression-level (1-9, default 7), rekey-after-bytes, rekey-after-seconds and minimum-rsa-bits; absent rekey-after-bytes uses the negotiated cipher's RFC 4344 volume limit, and absent rekey-after-seconds disables time-based rekeying.

Changing the ssh container reconnects the device. An algorithm name the SSH library does not support is rejected by the YANG enumeration; anything that slips past is logged and leaves the device disconnected rather than retrying a connection that can never come up.

The northbound NETCONF server has its own equivalent settings, configured as system settings rather than as intent; see Running StratoWeave.

items.title: Extra adapters
items.text:
A device can run more adapters beside the adapter of its device type, for what that adapter does not have. For example, a C8000V has no verify RPC over NETCONF, and a CLI adapter can give it. An extra adapter is a device type too, and the device entry lists it in extra-adapter:

src/sorespo/cfs.act
cli = dev.extra_adapter.create("CiscoIosXe_cli")
cli.port = u64(22)

Each adapter reports the modules it serves. A module belongs to the first connected adapter that has it: the adapter of the device type, then the extra adapters in their order. While no adapter that has it is connected, it belongs to the first that has it. Oper reads, subscriptions, RPCs and event notification subscriptions go to the adapters of the modules that their top-level nodes name, and move when a connection comes or goes. A module that no adapter has goes to the adapter of the device type, and so does all configuration.

The IOS XE CLI adapter also reads the BGP neighbors, into bgp-state-data of Cisco-IOS-XE-bgp-oper, as NETCONF gives them. A device whose NETCONF does not start, such as IOS XE 16.8 on a C1111, has them from the CLI; when NETCONF connects, NETCONF serves them. The CLI adapter realizes a subscription by reading again at each period, and has no on-change subscriptions.

An extra adapter connects to the address that its address leaf names, or to the first address. It uses its own port, or its default port when port is not set: the port of the address is for the adapter of the device type. Its credentials and its ssh settings, when set, replace the device's. Two SSH servers on one device can need different settings: on a C1111 with IOS XE 17.9, an RSA key needs public-key-algorithm ssh-rsa on the CLI port but not on the NETCONF port. state/adapter shows whether each adapter is connected.

An adapter runs as an extra adapter when it reports its device type with its modules, dev.on_connect(modules, schema_key, dmc.type), and a lost connection with dev.on_disconnect(dmc.type). A report without the device type is the one of the adapter of the device type.

items.title: Device logs
items.text:
Every device writes its own log file, devices/<name>.log in the log directory; see Running StratoWeave. The device logs at the level of the log.device.level setting, unless its debug/log-level leaf sets another level. With debug/connection set, the device logs at trace and the file also holds every NETCONF message to and from the device, configuration data included.

Like the other device settings, both leaves come from the transform that creates the device entry. To let operators change the level of one device at run time, expose the leaves in the northbound model and copy them, as the fleetmgr example does:

fleetmgr/src/fleetmgr/cfs.act
dev.debug.connection = i.debug.connection
dev.debug.log_level = i.debug.log_level

A new level applies without a reconnect.

items.title: RFS models still define the service-specific southbound data
items.text:
The built-in device list already comes from the StratoWeave RFS schema. Your project-specific RFS YANG augments that schema with the service-specific nodes that your RFS transforms need.

spec/yang/rfs/sorespo-rfs.yang
module sorespo-rfs {
    ...
    augment "/sw-rfs:rfs" {
        container base-config {
            sw:rfs-transform sorespo.rfs.BaseConfig;

            leaf name {
                type string;
            }
        }
    }
}

In other words, the layer above RFS creates both the device entry and the matching rfs subtree as part of the same overall intent. The generated device layer then uses the device entry to select the correct per-version adapter and reconcile the rendered configuration against the target device.

items.title: HTTP inspection API
items.text:
StratoWeave orchestrators expose a small HTTP inspection API rooted at /.

This API is useful for inspecting devices, layer state, configuration queues, and rendered southbound configuration.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
You can call these endpoints against any StratoWeave orchestrator with a base URL like this:

curl "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/device/AMS-CORE-1/running?format=xml"

A few conventions matter when you call these endpoints directly:

  • Device names in /device/<name>/... are case-sensitive.
  • The /device/<name>/* config endpoints select output format with the format query parameter.
  • The /layer/<idx> endpoint does not use ?format=. It selects output from the Accept header instead.
  • For Acton adata output, both /device/<name>/* and /layer/<idx> support a loose query parameter. It defaults to true.

items.title: SORESPO quicklab examples
items.text:
SORESPO quicklab Makefiles use these inspection endpoints today:

  • GET /layer/<idx>
  • GET /device/<name>/target?format=<fmt>
  • GET /device/<name>/running?format=<fmt>
  • GET /device/<name>/diff?format=<fmt>
  • GET /device/<name>/resync

Typical Make targets include:

make get-config0
make get-config-json2
make get-config-adata3
make get-target-ams-core-1
make get-running-ams-core-1
make get-diff-ams-core-1
make resync-ams-core-1

items.title: GET /device
items.text:
Returns the list of managed device names as JSON.

Example response:

{"devices":["AMS-CORE-1","FRA-CORE-1"]}

items.title: GET /device/<name>/info
items.text:
Returns device metadata and current orchestration state as JSON.

This includes:

  • device name and configured type
  • approval mode
  • configured addresses
  • configured username
  • has_running_config
  • has_target_config
  • queue_length
  • pending_approvals
  • feature flags
  • discovered module list

This is the best summary endpoint when you need to understand whether a device is configured, queued, or missing data.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/capabilities
items.text:
Returns device capabilities as JSON.

Example response shape:

{"capabilities":["urn:ietf:params:netconf:base:1.1"]}

items.title: GET /device/<name>/modules
items.text:
Returns the device module set as JSON.

Each module entry contains the module name, namespace, revision, and features. This is useful when you need to confirm the live schema seen by the device manager.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/running?format=<fmt>
items.text:
Returns the current running configuration known for the device.

Supported formats:

  • json
  • xml
  • gdata
  • adata

Example:

curl "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/device/AMS-CORE-1/running?format=xml"

If no running configuration is available, the endpoint returns a 200 with the plain-text message # No running configuration available.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/target?format=<fmt>
items.text:
Returns StratoWeave's target configuration for the device: the config the orchestrator wants the device to have.

Supported formats:

  • json
  • xml
  • gdata
  • adata

Example:

curl "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/device/AMS-CORE-1/target?format=xml"

If no target configuration is available, the endpoint returns a 200 with the plain-text message # No target configuration available.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/diff?format=<fmt>
items.text:
Returns the difference between running and target configuration for the device.

Supported formats:

  • json
  • xml
  • gdata
  • adata

Example:

curl "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/device/AMS-CORE-1/diff?format=xml"

If there is no diff, the endpoint returns # No differences. If either side is missing, it returns # Configuration not available.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/log?format=<fmt>
items.text:
Returns the device configuration event log as JSON.

Each log item contains:

  • timestamp
  • event
  • conf_diff

Supported diff renderings inside the JSON payload:

  • json
  • xml
  • gdata

adata is not implemented for this endpoint.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/q
items.text:
Returns the device's configuration queue as JSON.

The response is a map keyed by queue item id. Each value currently includes the transaction id.

Example response shape:

{
  "7": {"tid": "1234"},
  "8": {"tid": "1235"}
}

items.title: GET /device/<name>/q/<id>?format=<fmt>
items.text:
Returns one queue item in JSON, including the diff awaiting approval or application.

Fields include:

  • tid
  • config_diff
  • device_txid
  • format

Supported diff formats for this endpoint are narrower than the device config endpoints:

  • xml (default)
  • gdata
  • json returns # JSON diff not available
  • adata returns # Adata diff not available

items.title: POST /device/<name>/q/<id>/set_approval
items.text:
Sets approval for a queued device config item.

Request body:

{"device_txid":"abc123","approved":true}

Response:

{"status":"ok","approved":true}

This is the approval action behind configuration approval workflows such as the SORESPO queue UI.

items.title: GET /config-queue
items.text:
Returns all pending approvals across all devices as JSON.

Each device entry contains:

  • device_id
  • pending_count
  • items

Each item contains:

  • queue_id
  • tid
  • device_txid
  • approved

This is the best endpoint for a global approval queue view.

items.title: GET /device/<name>/resync
items.text:
Triggers a device resynchronization and returns a JSON acknowledgement.

Example:

curl "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/device/AMS-CORE-1/resync"

Response:

{"status":"ok","message":"Resync initiated"}

items.title: GET /layer/<idx>
items.text:
Returns the stored configuration for one StratoWeave layer.

Unlike the device config endpoints, serialization is selected with the Accept header:

  • application/yang-data+xml
  • application/yang-data+json
  • application/yang-data+acton-adata

The content query parameter selects what is returned, as in RESTCONF:

  • config (default): the configuration
  • nonconfig: the operational state the layer's transforms publish
  • all: both, merged into one tree

A layer with no operational state returns an empty document for nonconfig.

Examples:

curl -H "Accept: application/yang-data+xml" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/layer/0"

curl -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/layer/2"

curl -H "Accept: application/yang-data+acton-adata" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/layer/3?loose=true"

curl -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/layer/0?content=nonconfig"

The meaning of each layer index depends on the system specification.

For example, in SORESPO the layer numbers are:

  • 0: CFS
  • 1: Inter
  • 2: RFS
  • 3: Device

If the index is out of range, the endpoint returns 404.

items.title: Choosing the right endpoint
items.text: Use /layer/<idx> when you want to inspect StratoWeave's stored state at a specific transform layer. Use /device/<name>/target and /device/<name>/running when you want to compare the orchestrator's intended southbound device config with the device's current running config. Use /device/<name>/diff and /config-queue when you are diagnosing rollout or approval behavior.

items.title: Embedded static assets (web UI)
items.text:
Applications can embed a built web UI (or any set of text files) into their binary and have the HTTP server serve it alongside the APIs. Pass a static_assets map (URL path -> file content) to stratoweave.main(); it is forwarded to HttpServer and installed by the static_assets module.

Behavior:

  • Every asset is served on GET <path> on the same listener and port as the APIs. GET / serves /index.html when present. Assets are served by a catch-all GET /*path route that the router ranks below every static or parameterized route, so registered API routes always take precedence and can never be shadowed by an asset. Installing fails if the application already registered its own root-level GET wildcard.
  • Assets under /_app/immutable/ (content-hashed filenames) are served with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable; everything else with no-cache.
  • SPA fallback: a GET request that matches no route and carries an Accept header that explicitly allows text/html (a browser navigation) receives /index.html, so client-side routed pages survive a browser refresh. Requests without such an Accept header — API clients, curl — keep receiving a plain 404, and registered API routes always win over the fallback.
  • The flip side of route precedence: an asset whose path an existing GET route already matches — including parameterized and wildcard routes such as /device/{name}/info or /restconf/data/* — is unreachable. Keep asset paths (/index.html, /_app/...) out of the API namespace.

Limitations:

  • Only text assets can be served (response bodies are UTF-8 strings). Binary files such as images or fonts must be inlined by the frontend build, e.g. as data URIs.
  • HEAD is not supported by the HTTP server; use curl -sD- -o /dev/null rather than curl -I when inspecting response headers.

items.title: RESTCONF
items.text: StratoWeave orchestrators expose a standard RESTCONF interface rooted at /restconf for retrieving and modifying northbound service intent.

items.title: GET /.well-known/host-meta
items.text: Returns host metadata that points clients at the RESTCONF root.

items.title: GET /restconf/yang-library-version
items.text: Returns the advertised RESTCONF YANG library version.

items.title: GET /restconf/data
items.text:
Returns the top-level northbound data tree.

XML example:

curl -H "Accept: application/yang-data+xml" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/restconf/data"

JSON example:

curl -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/restconf/data"

items.title: Editing northbound intent
items.text:
The RESTCONF root is also used for configuration operations such as PATCH and DELETE.

For example, a StratoWeave orchestrator can accept northbound intent updates like this:

curl -f -X PATCH \
  -H "Content-Type: application/yang-data+xml" \
  -d @netinfra.xml \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/restconf/data"

JSON payloads can also be used:

curl -f -X PATCH \
  -H "Content-Type: application/yang-data+json" \
  -d @netinfra.json \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/restconf/data"

To remove a node, send DELETE to the resource path below /restconf/data:

curl -f -X DELETE \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/restconf/data/netinfra:netinfra/router=STO-CORE-1"

items.title: SORESPO quicklab examples
items.text:
SORESPO quicklab Makefiles use RESTCONF directly for both reads and writes. Typical targets include:

make get-config-restconf
make get-config-restconf-json
make send-config-wait FILE="netinfra.xml"
make send-config-json-wait FILE="netinfra.json"
make send-config-async FILE="netinfra.xml"

SORESPO quicklab also uses RESTCONF resource paths for simple validation, for example:

curl -sS -f -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  "$STRATOWEAVE_API_ORIGIN/restconf/data/netinfra:netinfra/router=AMS-CORE-1"

items.title: When to use RESTCONF vs the inspection API
items.text: Use RESTCONF when you want the northbound service model exactly as exposed by your orchestrator, or when you want to submit service intent. Use the StratoWeave inspection API for internal state such as layer snapshots, rendered per-device configuration, device module inventory, and approval queues.

items.title: Running StratoWeave
items.text: A StratoWeave-based Orchestrator is a single binary that can be deployed on any Linux-based system.

items.title: Deployment
items.text:
The simplest way to deploy a StratoWeave orchestrator is wrap up the binary into a container image and deploy it to a container orchestration platform such as Kubernetes. The following example shows a simple Dockerfile that wraps the SORESPO binary into a container image.

Dockerfile for a StratoWeave orchestrator
FROM ubuntu:22.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y libssh-4
COPY out/bin/sorespo /usr/local/bin/sorespo
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/sorespo"]

Tip

You could use a more minimal base image such as alpine or debian:slim, and in the future we intend to enable you to use a FROM scratch base image.

items.title: Logging
items.text:
StratoWeave writes one log file for each part of the system, in the directory logs below the working directory:

File Content core.log Startup and exit, TTT layers and transforms netconf.log Northbound NETCONF server: logins, sessions, subscriptions http.log HTTP server: RESTCONF, TMF API and web UI, one line per request at info devices/<name>.log One file per device: connection, configuration, software upgrades

The default level is warning, so a healthy system writes little. Startup messages are always written, at info, to core.log and to stdout: the log directory, the NETCONF listener and the startup configuration. So is the exit code when StratoWeave ends by itself, for example after --exit-on-done or a startup error. stdout also shows every message at the console level, which is log.level unless set.

system.aon
log:
    dir = "/var/log/sorespo"
    level = "warning"
    netconf:
        level = "info"
    device:
        level = "info"
Setting Default Meaning log.dir logs Directory for log files; empty to write no files log.level warning Level of every part without its own level log.core.level, log.netconf.level, log.http.level, log.device.level log.level Level of one part log.console.level log.level Level of stdout log.format text text or json log.rotate.size 10485760 Rotate a file when it reaches this many bytes; 0 to never rotate log.rotate.keep 5 Rotated files to keep for each log file

The levels are off, error, warning, info, debug and trace. The same settings are command-line options such as --log.level debug, and environment variables such as STRATOWEAVE_LOG__LEVEL.

A device can log at another level than the others: its debug/log-level overrides log.device.level, and debug/connection makes it log at trace. Both come from the device entry; see Device management.

items.title: Line format
items.text:
The text format writes one line for each message: the time with the UTC offset, the level, the part, the class and id of the actor that logged, the message, and its data as key=value pairs. Line breaks and other control characters are escaped, so a message is always one line.

2026-09-22T14:03:07.123456789+02:00 ERROR  rtr1: stratoweave.adapters.netconf.NetconfDriver[-439]: Device._on_connect: error connecting to device error="Connection refused"

The json format writes one JSON object for each line, with the keys time, level, logger, actor, actor_id, msg and, when the message has data, data. Use it when a log shipper sends the files to a search system.

Device configuration in debug messages leaves out the credentials.

items.title: Rotation
items.text:
When a file reaches log.rotate.size, it is renamed to <name>.log.1, the previous <name>.log.1 to <name>.log.2 and so on, and at most log.rotate.keep rotated files are kept.

To rotate with logrotate instead, set log.rotate.size to 0. StratoWeave opens the file for each write, so a file that logrotate moved away is created again on the next write. No signal and no copytruncate are necessary.

items.title: Containers
items.text:
In a container, mount a volume on the log directory, or set log.dir to an empty string to write no files. stdout then shows every message at log.level, and the container runtime captures it for docker logs or kubectl logs:

out/bin/sorespo --log.dir= --log.level info

items.title: Run-time configuration
items.text:
Running --help is the fastest way to confirm the exact interface exposed by the StratoWeave orchestrator binary you are using. The following example shows the output of --help for SORESPO, the reference implementation of a StratoWeave orchestrator.

Inspect runtime options for a StratoWeave orchestrator
out/bin/sorespo --help
Usage: sorespo [OPTIONS] [--] [FILE ...]

Arguments:
  FILE ...
      Startup configuration files, applied in order
      env: STRATOWEAVE_STARTUP_CONFIG_FILES; default: []

Options:
  --db TEXT
      TTT database: an LMDB path or a database URL
      env: STRATOWEAVE_DB; optional
  --exit-on-done / --no-exit-on-done
      Exit after startup config has been applied
      env: STRATOWEAVE_EXIT_ON_DONE; default: False
  --http.port INT
      HTTP listen port
      env: STRATOWEAVE_HTTP__PORT; default: 80
  --netconf.port INT
      NETCONF SSH listen port
      env: STRATOWEAVE_NETCONF__PORT; default: 830
  --netconf.user TEXT
      NETCONF SSH username (v1 static credential)
      env: STRATOWEAVE_NETCONF__USER; default: admin
  ...

Every setting has the same three spellings: a key in an AON settings file, an environment variable, and a command-line option. They resolve in that order, so the command line wins. Settings that belong to one subsystem share a path, which is a nesting in the settings file and a __ separator in the environment.

system.aon
db = "/var/lib/sorespo"
http:
    port = 8080
netconf:
    port = 1830
    user = "netops"

The FILE arguments are startup configuration documents, applied in the order given. Operators often keep a base system configuration in one file and add environment-specific overlays as later arguments.

The most important settings are:

  • --db enables persistence, taking either an LMDB directory or a database URL. Without it the orchestrator runs stateless and all configuration is lost on shutdown.
  • --http.port changes the HTTP listener, which defaults to 80.
  • --netconf.port changes the NETCONF over SSH listener, which defaults to 830.
  • --netconf.ssh.host-key points to a persistent SSH host key. If you omit it, an ephemeral in-memory key is generated at startup.
  • --netconf.user and --netconf.password configure the built-in static NETCONF credentials. They default to admin / admin and should be overridden outside local testing.
  • --exit-on-done applies the supplied startup configuration and then exits instead of continuing to serve traffic. This is useful for CI validation or one-shot initialization jobs.

items.title: NETCONF server SSH transport
items.text:
The SSH transport the northbound NETCONF server offers is configured under netconf.ssh. Leave it alone and the SSH library's defaults apply.

system.aon
netconf:
    ssh:
        cipher = ["aes256-gcm@openssh.com", "aes256-ctr"]
        host_key_algorithm = ["ssh-ed25519"]
        rekey_after_seconds = 3600

The same settings are --netconf.ssh.cipher on the command line, repeated once per value, and STRATOWEAVE_NETCONF__SSH__CIPHER in the environment.

The algorithm lists (cipher, mac, key_exchange, host_key_algorithm, public_key_algorithm, compression_algorithm) are ordered preference lists, most preferred first, and an empty one means the library default. The rest are compression_level (1-9, default 7), rekey_after_bytes, rekey_after_seconds and minimum_rsa_bits. Both rekey limits are optional: unset means no byte limit beyond the negotiated cipher's own, and no time-based rekeying.

An algorithm name the SSH library does not support fails at startup rather than on the first connection. The equivalent settings for connections to devices live in the device's ssh container, described in Device management.

items.title: Acton Runtime System
items.text:
As for any Acton application, you can also configure the Acton Runtime System.

Note

There is generally no need to change these settings, the defaults are suitable for most deployments.

items.title: Platform Reference
items.text: This section contains reference documentation for the StratoWeave platform. It includes detailed information on the platform's architecture, design principles, and how to use its features effectively.

items.title: Device platform
items.text: StratoWeave reads what each device is: its operating system family, its release, its chassis model and its serial number. A platform probe does the read. StratoWeave comes with probes, and an app can add its own or replace them.

items.title: Parts
items.text: Part Where Role PlatformProbe src/device.act Reads the platform of a device. GetPlatformProbe src/device.act A probe that needs one get. Most probes are one. platform_probes.PROBES src/platform_probes.act The probes that come with StratoWeave. platform_probes.MODELS src/platform_probes.act The YANG those probes read, for a device type that does not know the OS. The probes src/adapters/platform_<os>.act One module per OS, with its pruned YANG in platform_<os>_yang.act. ncurl platform src/ncurl.act Reads one device with PROBES and prints its platform. SysSpec.platform_probes src/app.act The app's list of probes. PROBES unless the app gives its own. DeviceType.platform_probes src/device.act Probes for devices of one type. They run before the app's list. DeviceMgr src/device.act Picks the probe, runs it and publishes the answer.

items.title: State
items.text:
Published under stratoweave-rfs:device=<name>/state/platform. Not persisted: after a restart it is empty until the device connects.

Leaf Meaning os Operating system family: ios-xe, ios-xr, junos, srlinux, sros or arcos. The probe sets it; it is not read from the device. version Release the device runs, as it reports it, for example 17.18.2. model Chassis model, for example C8000V. serial-number Chassis serial number. probe Name of the probe that read the values.

The version is the release as the device spells it, without what the device puts around it: the IOS XE banner, the v and the build of SR Linux, the image type of SR OS. Compare it with a release name through the platform's SoftwareAdapter.matches_release, not with ==: IOS XE reports 17.18.3a for an image called 17.18.03a.

items.title: When the platform is read
items.text:
• On every connect.
  • When a software install ends, also in a rollback, because the release can change without a reconnect.

Nothing polls. A box that is replaced comes with a new connection.

items.title: Which probe runs
items.text:
DeviceMgr walks this list and runs the first probe that applies:

device type's probes  +  app's probes (SysSpec.platform_probes)

A probe's applies looks only at the device's module set. So the same modules always pick the same probe, and no read is needed to pick it. There are no scores: when two probes apply, the one earlier in the list runs.

A device that lists its modules in its NETCONF hello, without yang-library or netconf-monitoring, also gets its other hello capabilities in its module set, named by their URI, but not the NETCONF protocol ones. A device from before YANG lists no modules, so these are what a probe can apply to.

The probe DeviceMgr does not apply tries the next probe in the list answers publishes the answer gives PlatformMismatch tries the next probe that applies fails, or gives no values keeps the values if this probe read them, else removes them, and runs the probe again after 5 seconds gives NotConnectedError stops; the next connect reads again
  • A probe that fails again waits twice as long each time, up to 300 seconds.
  • A failed read does not go on to the next probe. Two probes can spell the same model differently, so a value read by one probe would change each time the other one failed.
  • When no probe applies, the values are removed.
  • When the module set is empty, nothing is read and the values stay.
  • A reply or a retry from an earlier connection, or from the adapter the device had before a type change, is dropped.

PlatformMismatch is for a probe that applies by its modules but finds in the data that the device is not its case. An app's probe for one odd model can read, see a normal box and leave it to the default probe.

items.title: Choosing the probes for an app
items.text:
An app sets its list in <app>/device_types.act, next to its device types. The generated sysspec.act passes the list to SysSpec. The sysspec generator writes the file with this list when the file is missing:

import stratoweave.device as swdev
import stratoweave.platform_probes as swplat


device_types: dict[str, swdev.DeviceType] = {}

platform_probes: list[swdev.PlatformProbe] = swplat.PROBES

An app whose device_types.act was written before the list existed must add the import and the list itself. The generator does not change the file once it exists.

To Write Use the defaults swplat.PROBES Add a probe [my_probe] + swplat.PROBES Replace a default probe for some devices Put your probe first. Its applies picks the devices. Read no platform []

A device type can bring its own probes: DeviceType(..., platform_probes=[my_probe]). They run before the app's list, so an adapter package can ship the probe for its own devices, as a CLI adapter would: it knows which commands name the model. An app cannot put a probe before a device type's probes; to change them, give the device type other probes.

items.title: One get: GetPlatformProbe
items.text:
A subclass sets name and filt, and implements applies and parse. This is the IOS XE probe:

class IosXeProbe(swdev.GetPlatformProbe):
    def __init__(self):
        self.name = OS
        self.filt = platform_filter()

    def applies(self, modset: dict[str, ModCap]) -> bool:
        return MODULE in modset

    def parse(self, root: ?ygdata.Node) -> ?swdev.Platform:
        return platform(root)
Member Meaning filt Filter of the get. Select only what parse needs. applies(modset) Whether the probe can read a device with these modules. No I/O. parse(root) The Platform in the reply, None when the reply has no values, or raises PlatformMismatch.

Set the fields the probe knows on swdev.Platform(os, version, model, serial_number); leave the others None.

items.title: The device type's schema
items.text:
A probe reads through the device's schema: the one fetched from the device when runtime schema fetch is on, else the one the device type bundles. A bundled schema must have the nodes that the probe reads. A probe ships its pruned YANG next to its code, and the device type for that OS adds it, as fleetmgr/spec/src/gen.act does for IOS XE:

iosxe = swbuild.DeviceType.from_dir(fc, "iosxe", "yang/dev-iosxe")
iosxe.models.extend(swxe_yang.models)

When the schema lacks a node that the filter names, the get fails with Filter node <path> not found in device schema. The probe then runs again later, as after any failure.

items.title: More than one read: PlatformProbe
items.text:
For a probe that needs an RPC or more than one read, subclass PlatformProbe and implement applies and read(dev, done). read calls done once:

Call Meaning done(platform, None) The answer. done(None, PlatformMismatch()) The device is not the probe's case. done(None, error) The read failed.

read runs in the DeviceMgr, so it must not wait for the result of a call to dev: that call would wait for read to end. A reply from dev must go to an action, and a nested function in a class method is not one. So read starts an actor that sends the requests and receives the replies, one step after the other. The IOS XR probe's _IosXrRead and the SR Linux probe's _SrLinuxRead send two gets, the Junos probe's _JunosRead two RPCs.

Give each get one subtree. Some devices take only one subtree in a filter, so a probe that reads two subtrees sends two gets.

items.title: The probes
items.text:
Probe Applies when the device lists Reads Model Serial number ios-xe Cisco-IOS-XE-device-hardware-oper one get: inventory and version banner chassis part number chassis entry ios-xe-cli stratoweave-iosxe-cli, from the IOS XE CLI adapter one get: show version the word after cisco on the processor line Processor board ID ios-xr Cisco-IOS-XR-install-oper two gets: install/version, the rack inventory chassis-pid, else the rack's model the rack with the lowest name junos junos-rpc-version, or the capability http://xml.juniper.net/netconf/junos/1.0 RPCs get-software-information, get-system-information product-model serial-number of system information srlinux srl_nokia-system-info and srl_nokia-platform-chassis two gets: system/information, platform/chassis chassis type chassis sros nokia-state one get: /state/system and /state/chassis system/platform router chassis with the lowest number arcos arcos-openconfig-system-augments one get: system/version/state platform serial-number

Each probe but Junos reads through YANG that its module ships pruned in platform_<os>_yang.act (software_iosxe_yang.act for IOS XE), with the namespaces and node names of the real modules. A device type for that OS adds those models, unless its schema has the real modules. The probes apply to different modules, so a device's modules pick one of them, except an IOS XE device with both adapters: there ios-xe comes first and runs.

items.title: IOS XE
items.text:
• Takes the model and serial number from the chassis entry with the lowest hw-dev-index, so a stack gives the same answer whatever order the entries come in.
  • Takes the version out of the banner, as the software adapter does: the text after the first Version up to the comma. A c8000v 17.18.2 reports Cisco IOS Software [IOSXE], Virtual XE Software (...), Version 17.18.2, RELEASE SOFTWARE (fc3) and three more lines.

Cisco-IOS-XE-platform-oper names the chassis too, but a lab c8000v returned invalid UTF-8 in that tree.

IosXeSoftwareMock serves a chassis entry: part-number C8000V and serial number 9ABCDEFGHIJ, or the model and serial it is given. A mock device sets them as mock/platform/model and mock/platform/serial-number, and the release it starts on as mock/platform/version.

items.title: IOS XE over the CLI
items.text:
ios-xe-cli reads a device that has the IOS XE CLI adapter as an extra adapter. It comes after ios-xe in PROBES, so it reads only while the device's NETCONF has not connected, as on IOS XE 16.8 on a C1111, where the NETCONF server does not start. When NETCONF connects, ios-xe reads again and its values replace these.

It gives the release as the banner spells it, 17.15.6 where show version says Cisco IOS XE Software, Version 17.15.06, so the release stays the same when ios-xe takes over. The model and the serial number of a C1111 are the same in both.

items.title: IOS XR
items.text:
install/version holds what show version prints: the release label and, on some devices, the chassis-pid. The rack inventory in Cisco-IOS-XR-invmgr-oper holds what show inventory prints for Rack 0: its model and serial number.

  • An XRd has a chassis-pid, XRd-CP-C-01, and no inventory: the inventory get answers no data, so it has no serial number.
  • An XRv 9000 has no chassis-pid. Its model, R-IOSXRV9000-CC, and its serial number come from the inventory.
  • The inventory get is optional: when it fails, the probe still answers from install/version.

items.title: Junos
items.text:
Junos serves no state in YANG for what it is, so the probe calls the RPCs that show version and show system information call. Junos does not put an RPC's reply in the namespace of its YANG module, and runtime schema fetch skips the junos-rpc-* modules. So the probe sends the RPCs with rpc_xml and reads the replies by element name, and needs no YANG in the device type's schema. That also lets it read a Junos from before YANG, which lists no modules but has the Junos capability in its hello.

  • The model and the release come from get-software-information; a device with two routing engines answers for each, and the probe takes the first.
  • The serial number comes from get-system-information. When that RPC fails, the probe still answers, without a serial number. A cRPD has no serial number and leaves os-version empty.

items.title: SR Linux
items.text: The version is v25.3.2-312-ga0c5002f15: the probe drops the v and the build, which gives 25.3.2.

items.title: SR OS
items.text: The probe applies to a model-driven or mixed mode SR OS, which serves nokia-state. The version number starts with the image type: B-25.10.R7 on an SR-SIM gives 25.10.R7, C-23.10.R1 on a 7950 XRS vSIM 23.10.R1. A system of two chassis, like a 7950 XRS-40, lists both; the serial number comes from the router chassis with the lowest number.

items.title: ArcOS
items.text: system/version/state holds what show version prints. On a container the platform is Virtual and there is no serial number. The OpenConfig chassis component has neither part nor serial number there.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Test Covers src/test_platform.act Which probe runs and what DeviceMgr publishes, with fake probes: order, device type first, mismatch, failure, removal, every connect. src/adapters/test_platform_lab.act What virtual devices of each platform answered, recorded in test_platform_lab_data.act: which probe each device's module list picks, what each probe makes of the device's replies, and what DeviceMgr publishes when a mock NETCONF server serves them. src/adapters/test_platform_<os>.act Each probe's parse of replies not recorded there, like hardware with serial numbers and Junos with two routing engines, and applies. src/adapters/test_platform_iosxe.act Also the IOS XE filter and the error for a device type without the hardware module.

To add a platform, record a device's module list and its replies in test_platform_lab_data.act, and add it to test_platform_lab.act. The selection test then checks that no other probe applies to its modules, and that the new probe applies to no other device's.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• Retries have no jitter: devices that connected together retry together.
  • A probe that applies but cannot read retries every 300 seconds while the device stays connected: when the device never serves the data, or when the device type's schema lacks the module. Mocked devices without IosXeSoftwareMock never serve it.
  • An IOS XE reply with a version but no chassis entry is an answer, so it removes the model and serial number.
  • The mock NETCONF server's subtree filter returns no data at all when a node the filter selects is absent, where a device returns the other nodes. A mocked device must serve every node that the probe selects.
  • With runtime schema fetch on, ArcOS 8.2.1A gets no schema, so no probe reads it: an ArcOS module imports tailf-rollback, which ArcOS does not list.

items.title: Event Notifications
items.text:
Devices emit discrete events — an upgrade finished, a config changed out of band, a linecard appeared — modeled in YANG as notification statements. StratoWeave delivers them to subscribers as typed events, and can emit its own on the northbound NETCONF interface.

Event notifications are a separate lane from streaming telemetry: telemetry delivers a converging operational data tree, events are discrete and ordered. The two share wire machinery but have different APIs on purpose.

items.title: Subscribing to device events
items.text:
Declare a set of NotifSpec on a DeviceMgr (an RFS Transform Actor holds one as params.dev):

import adapters.adapter as swadapt
import yang.gdata as gdata

VERIFY_EVENT = gdata.Id("http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-verify-events",
                        "verify-event")

def on_event(ev: ?swadapt.NotifEvent, err: ?Exception) -> None:
    if ev is not None:
        ...  # ev.payload is the event decoded against the device schema

dev.declare_notif_subscriptions("my-owner", on_event,
                                {swadapt.NotifSpec(VERIFY_EVENT)})

A NotifSpec is a qualified notification name, optionally pinned to a device stream:

NotifSpec(VERIFY_EVENT)                     # one notification, routed by policy
NotifSpec(VERIFY_EVENT, stream="NETCONF")   # one notification, routing pinned
NotifSpec(stream="snmpevents")              # everything on one stream (a tap)
NotifSpec()                                 # everything on the default channels

Like telemetry subscriptions, the declaration is the owner's full desired state: each declare_notif_subscriptions call replaces the previous set, and remove_notif_subscriptions(owner_id) drops it. Two owners declaring the same spec share the underlying device subscription.

items.title: Waiting for the subscription
items.text:
An RPC can report its result as an event: IOS XE's verify returns a UUID, and the checksum arrives later in a verify-event with that UUID. Send such an RPC only once the subscription is in place, or the event can come before the device subscription exists and is lost. Pass synced to be told:

def on_synced(owner_id: str) -> None:
    ...  # the subscription is in place: send the verify RPC now

dev.declare_notif_subscriptions("my-owner", on_event,
                                {swadapt.NotifSpec(VERIFY_EVENT)}, on_synced)

synced is called once per declaration, when the device subscriptions for every spec are in place. If a subscription fails, the owner gets cb(None, err) instead.

items.title: What arrives
items.text:
Matching events arrive as cb(event, None) where a NotifEvent carries:

  • name: gdata.Id — the qualified notification name
  • event_time: str — the envelope's eventTime, verbatim RFC 3339 text
  • payload: ?gdata.Node — the event decoded against the device schema, or None when it is not in the schema or failed to decode
  • raw: xml.Node — the payload element as received, always present, with any namespace prefixes the device declared on the envelope

cb(None, err) signals channel trouble: the notification session dropped or a device rejected a subscription. It means you may be missing events until this recovers; recovery is automatic and silent.

Subscription machinery notifications — RFC 8639 subscription-state changes, RFC 5277's replayComplete/notificationComplete — belong to the adapter and are never delivered as events.

items.title: Delivery semantics
items.text:
Delivery is at-most-once with no replay. Events fired while a notification session is down are gone — unlike telemetry, events do not converge. Treat notifications as hints that accelerate your logic, not as a reliable stream: confirm outcomes through operational state where it matters, and use the error callback as the cue to fall back to polling.

Ordering is preserved per underlying channel; nothing is guaranteed across channels. An event matching several of one owner's specs is delivered once.

items.title: How it reaches the device
items.text:
Transforms never deal with mechanisms — that is adapter policy, inspectable via dev.notif_status(). For NETCONF devices the driver reconciles specs into channels:

  • Devices with RFC 8639 subscribed-notifications get establish-subscription on the main session (per-name stream-subtree-filter on the NETCONF stream).
  • IOS XE's draft dialect gets per-name establishes on the yang-notif-native stream for Cisco's native event modules, Cisco-IOS-XE-*-events and Cisco-IOS-XE-*-events-oper; IOS XE sends these only there. Other names fall back to RFC 5277.
  • Everything else uses classic RFC 5277 create-subscription on a dedicated session per stream — forced by 5277 itself: one anonymous subscription per session, no modify or cancel, and no other RPCs without :interleave.

Demux is always by notification name on our side; device-side filters are only bandwidth optimizations. That also means routing mistakes fail soft — but a name routed to a stream the device never emits it on is silent non-delivery. The stream pin on NotifSpec is the override for such cases, and an unfiltered tap is the discovery tool.

Mock devices support the same API: MockAdapter.inject_notif(name, payload, stream) delivers synthetic events with the same matching rules the real driver uses, and the NETCONF mock server's emit_event(...) exercises the full wire path.

items.title: Watching notifications with ncurl
items.text:
ncurl notifications subscribes through a DeviceMgr the way a transform does, and prints each notification as it arrives. Without --notification it prints all of them, which shows what a device sends and on which channel:

out/bin/ncurl --host router notifications
out/bin/ncurl --host router notifications --notification ietf-netconf-notifications:netconf-config-change
out/bin/ncurl --host router notifications --stream snmpevents --format raw

A notification is named module:name. The line on stderr says how the adapter subscribed, for example create-subscription stream=NETCONF (dedicated session, active). --count stops after that many notifications, and --yang-dir decodes them with local YANG files instead of downloaded schemas, as for ncurl monitor.

items.title: Automatic drift detection
items.text: When a device advertises ietf-netconf-notifications (RFC 6470), the DeviceMgr subscribes itself to netconf-config-change and triggers a resync on it — out-of-band configuration drift is detected the moment the device reports it, rather than on the next reconnect. IOS XE reports changes made from the CLI as well as over NETCONF.

items.title: Emitting notifications northbound
items.text:
StratoWeave's own NETCONF server serves RFC 5277 create-subscription and advertises the :notification and :interleave capabilities. Emitting is one call on the server's hub:

hub = netconf_server.event_hub()
hub.publish(payload)                      # NETCONF stream, timestamped now
hub.publish(payload, stream="my-stream")  # a stream declared with define_stream

payload is the notification's XML element (for gdata content, node.to_xml()). Every subscribed session whose stream and name filter match receives it; with no subscribers the event simply evaporates.

items.title: Current limitations
items.text:
• No replay: RFC 5277 startTime / RFC 8639 replay-start-time are not used yet.
  • Nested (YANG 1.1) notifications are identified by their top-level payload element, so they only reach unfiltered taps.
  • The northbound server does not serve RFC 8639 event-stream establish-subscription yet; the classic RPC covers the event side. It also does not serve the RFC 5277 /netconf/streams discovery container.
  • The automatic config-change resync does not yet discriminate changed-by, so StratoWeave's own commits trigger a redundant (harmless) resync on devices that emit RFC 6470 notifications.
  • IOS XE matches a yang-notif-native filter against the module's own prefix, which the adapter takes from the device schema. A notification whose module is not in the schema is rejected (error-no-such-option) and retried.

items.title: SNMP devices
items.text: An SNMP device type starts with its MIB modules. The system generator uses actsnmp to resolve the MIBs and translate them to YANG using RFC 6643. ActYang then generates the same operational data classes and subscription paths used for other device types.

items.title: Build a device type
items.text:
Use DeviceType.from_mibs in the system specification. This example runs from minisys/gen:

import stratoweave.build as swbuild

snmp_device = swbuild.DeviceType.from_mibs(
    fc,
    "ietf_snmp",
    ["mibs/ietf-snmp"],
    ["SNMPv2-MIB", "IF-MIB"],
)
spec = swbuild.SysSpec("mini", [cfs_layer, rfs_layer], [snmp_device])
spec.compile().gen_app(fc, "../src/")

The directory list is the MIB import search path. Imported MIBs are resolved automatically; the base SMI modules and textual conventions are bundled with actsnmp. Missing modules, MIB errors, and failed translations stop generation. The generator translates the MIBs to YANG in memory and generates Acton code directly from that translation, so only the source MIBs are committed. To inspect the translated YANG, set yang_dir="out/snmp-yang".

Alongside ietf_snmp.act, ietf_snmp_schema.act, and ietf_snmp_oper.act, generation writes ietf_snmp_mib.act. It holds the MIB metadata that the adapter reads by: object OIDs, table index encodings, textual conventions, and value conversions. It also defines the adapter function that the generated device registry uses for the device type. YANG and metadata come from one translation, so their paths agree. Generated application packages import actsnmp through this module and need the dependency:

"snmp": (
    follows="stratoweave.snmp"
),

The RFC mapping produces operational (config false) nodes. The adapter reads over SNMPv2c; configuration writes, notifications, on-change subscriptions, and SNMPv3 credentials are not exposed.

items.title: Subscribe from a transform
items.text:
Use the generated operational module's paths and a polling period in seconds:

import mini.devices.ietf_snmp_oper as snmp_oper
import yang.gdata as gdata

iface = snmp_oper.subs.IF_MIB.ifTable.ifEntry.entry(7)
want = {iface.subscribe(
    select=[iface.ifDescr, iface.ifOperStatus, iface.ifHCInOctets, iface.ifHCOutOctets],
    period=1.0,
)}
subs = gdata.SubscriptionManager(dev.tree_provider(), "interface-monitor")
subs.declare({snmp_oper.dst(on_state).deliver(want)})

The callback receives the typed tree rooted at the device data root. See Subscriptions for destination signatures and subscription lifetime.

items.title: Reads
items.text:
A row with a value for every INDEX key is read with GET, so the example above reads four OIDs. Leading key values narrow the walk of their table, and other tables are walked column by column in one pass. Scalars use the .0 OID suffix. Table indexes are decoded from each instance OID into YANG list keys, including keys that the agent marks not-accessible.

Each poll replaces the previous snapshot, so removed rows disappear. A failed poll reports an error and keeps the last successful tree. SNMP reads can span several requests and do not give an atomic snapshot of the device. Equal subscription declarations share a read, and reads never overlap within one stream. The adapter waits the requested period after each read completes. Each request waits 1 second and is retried twice. A table walk stops at 100,000 values and reports an error.

Configure an address, an optional port (default 161), and the SNMPv2c community in credentials/password. The adapter ignores the username; use an empty string because the shared schema requires it:

{
  "name": "router1",
  "type": "ietf_snmp",
  "address": [{"name": "management", "address": "192.0.2.1"}],
  "credentials": {"username": "", "password": "your-community"}
}

Changing the password reconnects the client with the new community.

items.title: Mini example
items.text:
The mini system's ietf_snmp device type uses SNMPv2-MIB and IF-MIB, vendored with the imported IANAifType-MIB in minisys/gen/mibs/ietf-snmp. The translated model preserves the MIB structure and names: interface rows are at IF-MIB/ifTable/ifEntry, and the ifXEntry augmentation adds the 64-bit counters to those rows. This is a different schema from the ietf-interfaces model of the mini ietf device type.

The RFS snmp-interface transform subscribes to the interface selected by if-index and publishes state/descr, state/oper-status, state/in-octets and state/out-octets. period-ms sets the polling period, and polling failures set state/error.

With mock/enabled, the adapter serves the device from an in-process SNMP agent that starts empty. Tests and scenarios seed it and change it between polls:

import snmp.oid as oid
import snmp.values as values

mock = adapter.get_mock_server()!
await async mock.set_bindings([
    values.VarBind(oid.Oid.parse("1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.7"), values.OctetString(b"Ethernet7")),
    values.VarBind(oid.Oid.parse("1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.7"), values.Integer(1)),
])
await async mock.set_value(oid.Oid.parse("1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.7"), values.Integer(2))

The suffix 7 becomes the ifIndex key, and the numeric status becomes the YANG enumeration (1 is up). Run the example from the repository root:

(cd minisys && acton test --module test_mini_snmp)

items.title: Software upgrades
items.text:
StratoWeave upgrades the software of each device on its own. You set the release a device should run, and the device's software manager moves the device to it. Which devices to upgrade, and when is decided by fleetmgr.

A release is one name per device, for example 17.18.03a. Platforms that version parts of their software separately are not supported yet.

items.title: Parts
items.text:
Part Where Role SoftwareManager src/device.act One per device. Runs the upgrade steps in order and publishes their state. SoftwareAdapter src/device.act One per platform. Does the device work for each step. Checks your application Decide if an upgrade may start, and if the new release may stay.

Every DeviceMgr owns one SoftwareManager. A device type names its adapter with software_adapter_type. A device type without one gets NoSoftwareAdapter, so its upgrades fail with "device type has no software adapter".

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Set under stratoweave-rfs:device=<name>/software:

Leaf Meaning target-release Release the device should run. Setting it makes the manager read the device, and upgrade it if no veto holds the install. image-url URL the device downloads the image from.
