The last part of the path is the file name on the device. veto[holder] While any entry exists, no install starts. The manager still reads the device. An install already running goes on. upgrade-campaign Campaign whose intent this is. The manager answers each attempt at target-release in this campaign as an entry of state/attempt. attempt A number, 0 by default. A new value is a new attempt: the manager reads the device again, and runs a failed upgrade again. A run of another attempt that is under way finishes first. allow-staging While a veto holds the install, prepare the target once per attempt: copy its image to the device ahead of the window.

The manager acts when target-release, upgrade-campaign, attempt, allow-staging or a veto changes, when the device type changes, and when the device connects. A new image-url alone does not make it act. A status that ends a read or a run (up-to-date, succeeded, failed, rolled-back or not-started) stands for its attempt. A reconnect, another config change, a new device type, or target-release removed and set again does not run the attempt again. To run a failed upgrade again, change attempt.

items.title: Upgrade steps
items.text:
check ──> already on target ──> up-to-date
  │
  ├─> a veto holds the install ──> upgrade-needed ──> with allow-staging: prepare once
  │
  └─> prepare ─> pre-checks ─> install ─> post-checks ─> commit ─> cleanup ─> succeeded
         │           │            │            │            │
         └───────────┴────────────┴─> failed   └────────────┴─> rollback ─> rolled-back
Step What happens check Read the running release. If it is the target, stop with up-to-date. If a veto holds the install, stop with upgrade-needed, and with allow-staging prepare the target once. If the read fails, go on, but see the rules. prepare Copy the image to the device. No outage. pre-checks Ask every pre-check. A refusal, or no answer within 60 seconds, ends with failed. Nothing is activated. install Activate the new release. The device reboots. The step ends when the device runs the target. post-checks Ask every post-check. A refusal, or no answer in time, starts a rollback. commit Tell the device to keep the new release. Then read the release again and re-read the device config. cleanup Remove the software that the device does not run, which makes room for the next upgrade. A failed cleanup leaves the run succeeded, with the error in reason. rollback Go back to the release the device ran before.

Rules:

  • An error in prepare or install ends with failed. A failed install does not roll back.
  • A failed commit starts a rollback. A failed rollback ends with failed. It can leave the device on the release that the run installed, uncommitted, and a read would take that for the target. So the attempt that the configuration names then, when it is another attempt, does not start: it answers not-started, and its reason names the attempt that failed.
  • If the device does not run the target after the commit, the run ends with failed. This happens when the device went back on its own before the commit arrived.
  • Post-checks get 15 minutes. When the platform goes back on its own after a set time (IOS XE does), the limit is cut so the commit is sent at least 2 minutes before that. With less than 2 minutes left, the manager rolls back at once.
  • A device runs one upgrade at a time. A change of intent during a run is taken up when the run ends.
  • Under a veto, a read that fails gives unknown, with the error in reason. If the device was not connected, the manager reads it again when it connects; after another error, after 5 seconds, then twice as long each time, up to 5 minutes. Without a veto, a device that is not connected gives unknown too, and is read again when it connects; another read error goes on to the upgrade, which reports what fails.
  • Right before the install, after the pre-checks, the manager looks at the config again. A veto now holds the install, with upgrade-needed and the holders in reason. A changed or removed target, or a changed campaign, ends the run with upgrade-needed and says so in reason; a new target or campaign is read then. A new attempt does not stop the run. The install installs the release the run read the device for.
  • Run state lives in memory. After a restart the state has no attempts, and the stored config makes the manager read the device again.

items.title: Checks
items.text:
Applications add checks by name. Every check must pass.

def precheck(done: action(bool, str) -> None) -> None:
    if peer_is_up:
        done(True, "peer up")
    else:
        done(False, "redundant peer is down")

swmgr = dev.get_swmgr()
swmgr.add_precheck("my-app", precheck)
swmgr.add_postcheck("my-app", postcheck)

A check gets a done action and calls it once it has decided, so it can do other work first. The manager passes it no device data; the check reads the device itself. A check added during a run counts from the next run. remove_precheck and remove_postcheck take a check out, also during a run. An answer that arrives after its round has ended is ignored.

The BGP device-health check in fleetmgr/src/flotilla/rfs.act is a working example.

items.title: State
items.text:
Published under stratoweave-rfs:device=<name>/software/state:

Leaf Value upgrade-campaign, target-release The campaign and the target of the attempts: those of the read or run that answered them, not the configuration of the moment attempt[number] One entry for each attempt that the manager has answered at that target in that campaign, with the leaves below. The first answer for another campaign or target starts the list over attempt/status unknown, up-to-date, upgrade-needed, in-progress, succeeded, failed, rolled-back or not-started attempt/stage The step the attempt's run is in, or the step it ended in attempt/reason Why the run failed or rolled back, why the release could not be read, or what held the install attempt/precheck, attempt/postcheck verdict (not-run, pass or fail), detail, and at, the time of the verdict attempt/job[prepare] The attempt's last prepare: state (running, done or failed), release, started, ended and, when it failed, message. While it runs, message says what the device does, as the adapter reports it, and an adapter that transfers the image sets progress in percent of image-size and message with the bytes attempt/job[install] The install of the attempt's run, with the same leaves. While it runs, message says what the device does, for example add: extract or waiting for the device to boot. After the install, until the run commits or rolls back, it says when the commit window ends, for example commit window ends 23:07 UTC veto[holder] The vetoes of the configuration, with their reason, so that a campaign sees the vetoes of other holders

The release the device runs is state/platform/version (see device-platform.md). The manager reads the platform again when an install ends, also after a rollback.

Every change goes into the device's operational data, so reads and oper subscriptions see it right away. A run of an attempt that a veto held removes its reason and sets both verdicts back to not-run. A new attempt is a new entry, and the entries of the earlier attempts stay. Removing target-release keeps the state. State is not saved; after a restart it has no attempts.

A prepare under a veto runs once per attempt, and again after a restart. Its result is only in the attempt's job[prepare]: a failed prepare leaves the status upgrade-needed, and is not run again, also not when allow-staging goes off and on. Turning allow-staging off does not stop a prepare that runs. When the veto goes, the run prepares again, since the IOS XE adapter copies the image every time, and fills the same job entry.

items.title: Adapter API
items.text:
A platform adapter is a subclass of SoftwareAdapter in src/device.act.

Method Does check(done) Read the running release. matches_release(running, target) Whether two names mean the same release. The default compares strings. prepare(done, release) Copy the image to the device. install(done, release) Activate the release. Call done only once the device runs it. commit(done) Keep the activated release. commit_window(done) Seconds left before the device goes back on its own, or None. rollback(done, previous) Go back to previous. Call done only once the device runs it. cleanup(done) Remove old images. The manager calls it after the commit, once the device runs the target. plan_estimate() Seconds a whole upgrade takes, for planners. Static. prepare_estimate() Seconds the copy of the image takes, for planners. Static. supports_mocking() Whether the adapter works with the device mock.

Jobs report through done. The error message becomes the run's reason, so it should name the operation and the device's cause, for example add failed: install-verify-pkg-fail.

While prepare or install runs, the adapter can tell the device's SoftwareManager (dev.get_swmgr()) what the device does: report_step(message) sets the job's message, and report_transfer(transferred, total) its progress and the bytes.

items.title: IOS XE
items.text:
IosXeSoftwareAdapter in src/adapters/software_iosxe.act runs each step over NETCONF when the device has the module for it, and over the IOS XE CLI adapter when the device has that as an extra adapter and lacks the module, as IOS XE 16.8 on a C1111 lacks NETCONF. It plans from the adapters that are connected, so after a reload a step runs over whichever adapter is back. Before it stages, it waits for an adapter that is not connected until that adapter has been without a connection for 2 minutes. An adapter that never connects, like NETCONF on 16.8, holds up only the first stage of an upgrade.

Step NETCONF CLI read the release software-version in Cisco-IOS-XE-device-hardware-oper show version read the versions install-version-state-info show install summary list bootflash Cisco-IOS-XE-platform-software-oper dir bootflash: check the image none verify /sha512, verify /md5, or verify for the signature prepare xcopy from image-url to bootflash copy install install (add only), then activate with a 30 minute auto-abort timer install add, then install activate auto-abort-timer 30 commit install-commit install commit rollback abort install abort cleanup remove of the inactive software install remove inactive
  • An <ok/> reply only means the device accepted the RPC. The adapter then reads install-oper-data for the records with its UUID until the operation ends. A CLI command returns when it ends, or when the session ends as the device reloads.
  • activate names the image by the version the device gave it during the add, for example 17.18.03a.0.5540.
  • The device reboots after activate and after abort. Read errors during the reboot are expected. The adapter reads the running release until it is the one it waits for.
  • Without install-commit within 30 minutes of activate, the device goes back to the old release on its own. 30 is the lowest value IOS XE accepts.
  • Releases are compared part by part, so 17.18.03a matches 17.18.3a.
  • Operation records are read every 10 seconds for up to 30 minutes. During a reboot the release is read every 20 seconds for up to 35 minutes. Nothing is retried.
  • Prepare keeps an image that is on bootflash and passes its check, and transfers one that is missing or fails it. Install checks it again, unless the image passed the same check and dir bootflash: shows the index, size and date that it had then, as stat would: a file written again, also deleted and copied anew, gets another index. A check of a 735 MB image takes about a minute on a C1111. The driver keeps the checks in memory: after a restart it checks again.
  • While the image transfers, the adapter reports how far it is: over NETCONF from the size of the file on bootflash at each poll of the xcopy, over the CLI from the marks that copy prints, one ! per 196608 bytes over http (measured on 16.8.1 and 17.15.06). The CLI adapter answers a read of copy-progress from what the running copy printed, without a command.
  • While the install runs, the adapter reports its step: over NETCONF the txn-cmd of the last transaction that the operation began, without install-txn-, as add: extract or activate: reload; over the CLI the last step line that the install command printed, as Performing Add on Active/Standby, from a read of install-progress. During a reboot the step is waiting for the device to boot. The check and the transfer of the image are steps too.
  • Before a transfer, bootflash needs 2.2 times the image-size of the intent: the image, and the packages that the add makes of it. Without the room, the adapter removes the inactive software once and looks again.
  • With the CLI adapter, install refuses to start when the running configuration has changes that write memory has not saved, because the reboot would lose them.
  • A device in bundle mode, which booted a .bin, takes no install add alone. Over the CLI the adapter converts it: boot system names packages.conf and then the running image, write memory saves that, and install add file ... activate commit adds, activates and commits in one command. That release has no commit window and no abort.
  • A device that runs IOS XE 16 in install mode installs with the same one command, over the CLI. On a C1111 with 16.8.1, install activate with the auto-abort timer waited until its SSH session closed, and from 17.9.5a install abort back to 16.8.1 failed, so a commit window cannot take the device back. A release that it has added is removed first: the one command adds it again from the image file.

The YANG for these RPCs and oper nodes is a trimmed copy in src/adapters/software_iosxe_yang.act. The bindings generated from it are in software_iosxe_rpc.act and software_iosxe_oper.act.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
File Tests src/test_swmgr.act The manager, with the in-memory adapter from src/adapters/software_mock.act src/adapters/test_software_iosxe.act The IOS XE adapter, against IosXeSoftwareMock

IosXeSoftwareMock in src/adapters/software_iosxe_mock.act runs behind the in-process NETCONF mock server. Like a real device, it answers an RPC before the work is done. It also serves one BGP neighbor for checks to read. A mock device sets these leaves under mock/software:

Leaf Meaning upgrade-duration Seconds a whole upgrade takes. Absent or 0 ends each step at once. upgrade-duration-variance Percent by which each upgrade's duration can differ from upgrade-duration, either way. Each upgrade draws its duration evenly in that range when its xcopy starts. Default 20; 0 makes every upgrade exact. failure One device failure to reproduce, see below.

mock/platform/version is the release before the upgrade. Default 17.18.02, which the mock reports as 17.18.2, as a device does.

The upgrade duration is split in the shares measured on a lab c8000v with a 962 MB image: copy 130 s, add 20 s, activate 240 s and commit 5 s, 395 s in all. An abort takes 240 s.

failure What the device does Run ends download-failed The copy fails after xcopy was accepted failed add-failed The add fails after install was accepted failed activate-refused activate is rejected failed commit-failed The commit fails after install-commit was accepted rolled-back reverts The timer ran out before the commit failed bgp-down BGP is down from the start, so a BGP pre-check refuses failed bgp-lost BGP is down on the new release, so a BGP post-check refuses rolled-back

items.title: Subscriptions
items.text: A subscription declaration pairs a set[yang.gdata.SubscriptionSpec] with a destination using dst.deliver(want). A yang.gdata.SubscriptionManager reconciles the resulting set of deliveries.

items.title: Monitoring With Local YANG Files
items.text:
ncurl monitor --yang-dir DIR loads a schema from local .yang files when the server does not serve its schemas, or when you want to supply them yourself. It scans the directory and its subdirectories, compiles the schema before connecting, and disables schema downloads. The local schema is used both to parse updates and to resolve --filter-subtree. It works with periodic monitoring and with --on-change.

For example, from the repository root, monitor a minisys server using its CFS models:

out/bin/ncurl --port 8830 --password admin monitor --yang-dir minisys/gen/yang/cfs

All local modules are selected by default. To select particular roots, use --module or the existing named --module-set groups. Their transitive imports and includes are added automatically:

out/bin/ncurl --host router monitor --yang-dir schemas --module ietf-system

Explicit modules and module sets are combined. These monitor options require --yang-dir; they select the schema, while --filter-subtree selects the data to monitor. The bundled stratoweave, ietf-inet-types, and ietf-yang-types modules supply missing imports only. A module found on disk takes precedence over its bundled copy.

Repeated identical files are deduplicated. When several revisions are available, select --module name@YYYY-MM-DD, or let an import/include's revision-date select the revision. Ambiguous sources, conflicting revision requests, missing modules, and unreadable or malformed files are errors. Loading errors stop the command before it connects.

items.title: Declaring Subscriptions
items.text:
SubscriptionManager is the owner-scoped declarative API. It binds:

  • one TreeProvider
  • one stable owner id
  • a set of destinations, each with its own callback

Each destination receives one merged gdata tree or, when rooted at a node, one instance of that node per call.

The public shape is intentionally small:

import yang.gdata as gdata
import mini.devices.ietf_oper as ietf_oper

subs = gdata.SubscriptionManager(
    dev.tree_provider(),
    "base-config",
)
dst = ietf_oper.dst(on_state)

want = set([
    ietf_oper.subs.system_state.clock.subscribe(depth=1, period=0.05)
])

subs.declare({dst.deliver(want)})

items.title: Generated Subscription Helpers
items.text:
Generated operational device modules such as mini.devices.ietf_oper also expose a typed path API for building subscription filters. The generated _oper module combines the config-false operational adata tree with the SubscriptionNode helpers used for subscriptions.

Start from the generated root:

import mini.devices.ietf_oper as ietf_oper

sub = ietf_oper.subs

The generated module builds one shared filter path tree as the subs module constant, rather than constructing a fresh helper tree for each use.

items.title: Subscribe To A Whole Subtree
items.text:
Call subscribe(...) directly on a path to subscribe to everything below that node:

# /system-state/clock
spec = sub.system_state.clock.subscribe(period=0.05)

items.title: Subscribe To Direct Children Only
items.text:
Use depth=1 when you want the direct children of a container or list entry, rather than the whole subtree:

# /system-state/clock/current-datetime
# /system-state/clock/boot-datetime
spec = sub.system_state.clock.subscribe(depth=1, period=0.05)

depth currently only supports 1.

items.title: Subscribe To One Keyed List Entry
items.text:
Use entry(...) on generated list paths to add key predicates without writing FNode filters manually:

iface = sub.interfaces.interface.entry("eth0")

# /interfaces/interface[name="eth0"]
spec = iface.subscribe(period=1.0)

items.title: Select Specific Children
items.text:
Use select=[...] to keep the list entry or container as the anchor, but only subscribe to specific descendants below it:

iface = sub.interfaces.interface.entry("eth0")

spec = iface.subscribe(
    select=[iface.statistics, iface.ipv4],
    period=1.0,
)

Every selected path must be below the anchor used for subscribe(...).

items.title: Merge Overlapping Descendants
items.text:
Selected descendants from the same subtree are merged into one filter:

iface = sub.interfaces.interface.entry("eth0")

spec = iface.subscribe(
    select=[
        iface.statistics.in_octets,
        iface.statistics.out_octets,
    ],
    period=1.0,
)

This produces one statistics branch with both leaves below it.

items.title: Inspect The Raw Filter
items.text:
Use filt() when you want the raw FNode without immediately wrapping it in a SubscriptionSpec:

clock_filt = sub.system_state.clock.filt()
spec = gdata.SubscriptionSpec(clock_filt, period=0.05)

This is useful in tests and when integrating with older code that still constructs SubscriptionSpec directly.

items.title: Declare Multiple Filters For One Owner
items.text:
SubscriptionManager still works on a set of SubscriptionSpec objects, so you can mix several generated filters in one declaration:

iface = sub.interfaces.interface.entry("eth0")

want = set([
    sub.system_state.clock.subscribe(depth=1, period=0.05),
    iface.subscribe(select=[iface.statistics, iface.ipv4], period=1.0),
])

subs.declare({dst.deliver(want)})

items.title: Where A Destination Is Rooted
items.text:
A destination decides where each delivered tree starts. The module-level dst is rooted at the top: the callback receives the whole subscribed tree, as above. Every generated container and keyed list has a dst of its own, rooted at that node: the callback receives one instance of the node at a time. Its arguments are the keys of every list on the way down, as a named tuple with a field per key named after the list and the key; the instance itself, typed, or None when it is gone; and an error, as on the top-rooted callback. A node with no list above it has no keys argument. The types come with the dst, so the callback needs no annotations.

import mini.layers.y_1_oper as y1_oper

def on_device(keys, device, err):
    if err is not None:
        ...
    elif keys is not None:
        if device is None:
            forget(keys.device_name)    # the device is gone
        else:
            record(keys.device_name, device)

def on_synced():
    ...                             # every device held at declaration has been delivered

dev = y1_oper.subs.device
subs.declare({
    dev.dst(on_device).deliver({
        dev.subscribe(period=1.0),
    }),
}, synced=on_synced)

Rooted below another list, the keys tuple carries that list's keys too: a destination at devices.device.interfaces.interface hands its callback keys.device_name, keys.interface_name and the interface.

The first pass delivers every instance the filter selects, one call each, and then calls synced. Every periodic read delivers all selected instances and reports instances removed since the last read. On-change, each change delivers the instances it touched, one per callback. The filters handed to a rooted destination must lead to its node, and they are read on one period or served on-change, not both. A destination rooted at a container receives that container, or None when it is gone.

synced belongs to the declaration, not to one destination: it is called once, when every delivery in that declare has had its first pass, the first read of each spec. A first read that ends in an error still counts: the error, then synced. A declaration that adds nothing new installs the new callbacks and nothing more: nothing is delivered again and synced fires at once, since there is nothing to wait for. TTT layers and device providers serve the same rooted destinations and complete the first pass even when the selected tree is empty.

When a provider declaration keeps its owner id and delivery root, its new baseline also reports removals for instances that leave the selection. This holds when the filter, period or mode changes. The public manager assigns a new child owner when a delivery's subscription set changes.

At the gdata level the root is an FNode path with one child per level and no predicates, carried by Dst(deliver, root=...); the destination stamps it on the specs it delivers, so two destinations with the same filters but different roots are served apart. A rooted delivery is a spine: a tree from the top down to the one instance, every list on the way holding one entry with its keys, with an Absent holding its keys where a list entry is gone and nothing where a container is gone. gdata.instances splits a tree into such spines and gdata.gone turns one into the report of its instance gone. A generated dst wraps the callback in an actor that converts the spine to the keys and the instance first; the provider sends each spine to it, so the conversion runs in that actor and not in the provider. After an owner's first pass the provider calls synced with the owner id, sent after the data so it arrives after it; the manager counts those for the declaration.

items.title: On-Change Subscriptions
items.text:
Omitting period creates an on-change SubscriptionSpec:

spec = sub.system_state.clock.subscribe(depth=1)

On a TTT layer an on-change subscription carries the operational state the layer's transforms publish with update_oper, and nothing else: no config, except the keys of the list entries the state sits under. What a transform passes to update_oper replaces its whole contribution; None removes it.

The delivery contract:

  • The first delivery is the complete baseline, and may be None when no transform under the filter has published yet. A consumer must accept that.
  • After the baseline every update_oper under the filter is delivered as it happens, in the order the layer received them, with the tree rebuilt along the changed path and everything else shared by reference. An update that leaves a transform's filtered slice unchanged is not delivered.
  • On-change and periodic filters of one consumer are delivered as one view. Rooted at a node, each change delivers the instances it touched.
  • A list entry joins the subscription when its transaction commits, never while it is provisional. TTT does not clear a transform's oper when its config is removed: the transform actor does, from its shutdown, with update_oper(None), and the entry leaves the tree.
  • Oper is not transactional: a commit that touches several entries can be seen entry by entry, and a config change and an oper push can race.
  • A filter that the tree cannot route, such as a content predicate on a container entry that would span several transforms, is reported once as an error and the subscription is dropped.

Both TTT and device providers decide on-change from period alone. The legacy on_change field on SubscriptionSpec does not select the mode. The NetconfDriver accepts on-change only against a device that pushes natively; a device without YANG-Push reports an error instead of polling.

items.title: Periodic Subscriptions
items.text:
Every successful periodic read delivers the subscribed data tree to the callback. Device subscriptions deliver each periodic YANG-Push snapshot. A transform actor can use these callbacks to track when a sample was received.

With several periods, each completed read delivers its tree merged with the latest trees from the other reads and any on-change subscription. Only the completed read has been refreshed; the other parts keep their previous samples. A read error is reported through the callback's error argument, so it can be distinguished from a fresh sample.

items.title: SubscriptionSpec
items.text:
SubscriptionSpec contains:

  • filt: ?FNode
  • period: ?u64

There is no explicit subscription mode. The behavior is inferred from period:

  • period is None: on-change subscription
  • period is not None: periodic subscription

Internally, period is normalized to nanoseconds and stored as ?u64. gNMI uses nanoseconds, so we can express that granularity natively.

items.title: Accepted period input
items.text:
The constructor accepts:

  • float: interpreted as seconds
  • u64: interpreted as nanoseconds
  • int: interpreted as nanoseconds
  • None

Any other type raises ValueError.

Examples:

# Periodic, 50 ms
yang.gdata.SubscriptionSpec(filt, period=0.05)

# Periodic, 50,000,000 ns
yang.gdata.SubscriptionSpec(filt, period=u64(50000000))
yang.gdata.SubscriptionSpec(filt, period=50000000)

# On-change
yang.gdata.SubscriptionSpec(filt)

The recommended style is to use float seconds for readability unless you specifically want to work in raw nanoseconds.

items.title: Declaration Model
items.text:
SubscriptionManager owns one logical subscriber. Each declare(...) call describes the full desired subscription set for that owner.

  • unchanged declarations are a no-op
  • removed subscriptions are removed automatically
  • added subscriptions are created automatically

Each destination receives the view selected by its subscriptions: a merged tree at the top, or complete individual instances at its delivery root.

items.title: Northbound On-Change
items.text: The northbound NETCONF server serves on-change YANG-Push from a TTT layer, for the operational datastore: a push-update with the baseline when sync-on-start is asked for, then one push-change-update per change. Its yang-patch is built from the change itself, with no tree diff: a replace of the changed transform's subtree, so omitted descendants disappear at the client, or a remove of the node that emptied, so a deleted list entry is one edit. Targets are module-qualified from the served schema. A failure while serving ends the subscription with subscription-terminated. A non-zero dampening-period and excluded change types are rejected.

items.title: Internal Model
items.text:
SubscriptionManager is the declarative owner-facing API. Below it, a TTT layer serves each consumer from a Subscription actor of the consumer's own, outside the Layer actor. The consumer's filters fold into one read per period: the union of the filters declared with that period, read in one pass. Each read runs on its period and delivers the subscribed view. Every delivery is the reads' latest trees merged into one view, sent straight to the consumer, by reference when there is one read. The Layer keeps only which actor serves which consumer.

The consumer's on-change filters fold into one subscription in the tree. This is telemetry, apart from the link subscriptions that carry config between transforms: nothing in it is transactional or waits. The actor walks the layer's tree once to lay it: each node answers with its path, its oper slice if it is a producer, and the children to continue with. A container transposes the filter and decides predicates on its own keys; a list selects entries by exact key or all of them and keeps the subscription so entries that commit later join it; a transform keeps it and answers its slice. The answers become the actor's shadow of the subscribed part of the tree, and the end of the walk is the baseline. After that every producer under the subscription pushes its slice to the actor as it changes, when it changed; the actor rebuilds the shadow along the changed path, shares everything else by reference, and delivers the view with the reads' latest trees merged in. A consumer that asks for it, the northbound NETCONF server does, gets each change alone first: the path of the node that changed with what it held before and after. TTT does not clear a transform's oper when its config goes: the transform actor does, from its shutdown, with update_oper(None), and the entry leaves the view. The subscription is laid again only when its filter changes.

Each declare(...) call is the consumer's complete desired state. The actor drops the reads and the subscription no longer wanted, starts changed ones over, keeps the rest with their latest trees, and calls synced once every read of the declaration has run and its subscription has been laid.

A consumer rooted at a node has one read, or one subscription in the tree. Each read delivers every selected instance and reports instances removed since the last read. Each on-change update delivers the instances it touched. Every instance is delivered as a tree from the top down to that instance.

items.title: Device Providers
items.text:
Both providers use Subscription for one destination's callbacks and declaration state. A device DeviceStream is one folded read or native stream shared across destinations. TTT's Read serves a periodic filter; its on-change route retains producer slices in a Shadow. Devices retain rooted state in an InstanceTree and apply incoming patches to it.

Device providers fold a destination's filters into one read per period and one on-change stream, using the same selection and root validation as TTT. Equal folded subscriptions share their device stream. Every successful periodic snapshot is delivered. A destination at the top receives the latest reads merged in period order, followed by the on-change state; with one read, its tree is passed directly.

A rooted device stream retains instances indexed by the keys on the path to its root. Its initial snapshot and periodic reads deliver each selected instance, followed by removals. A native on-change patch updates only the branches it names and delivers each changed instance's complete selected state once. Replacing or removing an ancestor visits the instances under that ancestor. No whole feed is assembled for rooted delivery.

The first result of every folded read, including errors and empty snapshots, completes the declaration's first pass. A new consumer of an existing stream receives its retained baseline before synced. Redeclaring an unchanged active stream replaces callbacks without replaying data. Closing one consumer keeps a shared stream alive for the others.

An establishment failure drops the device stream, so the same provider declaration can retry it. An on-change update that cannot be parsed or applied also drops the stream: later changes cannot repair a missed update. Every consumer receives the error and must treat its retained state as invalid. Redeclaring starts or joins a new stream and obtains a complete baseline before changes resume. A periodic read error keeps the stream; its next successful snapshot delivers the selected state again.

Transport capabilities determine how device reads run: periodic YANG-Push when supported, otherwise periodic NETCONF reads; native YANG-Push for on-change. Native YANG-Push periods are rounded down to whole centiseconds with a minimum of one centisecond. Delivery roots are local to the provider and do not require one wire subscription per instance.

items.title: YANG to Acton compilation
items.text:
The YANG to Acton compilation phase turns a StratoWeave system specification and its YANG models into the Acton modules used by transform code and the runtime. Run it after changing the system specification, a YANG model, a device type, or a device schema filter:

Compile YANG to Acton
make gen

The project's generator entry point, for example spec/src/sorespo_gen.act, loads the YANG models for each transform layer and device type, compiles the system specification, applies any schema filters, and calls gen_app(...). Generated files are written below the project's source package. They should not be edited by hand.

items.title: Transform layer modules
items.text:
Each transform layer produces five modules in src/<project>/layers/. The number in the module name is the layer's position in the system specification, starting with layer 0 at the top of the transform stack.

Module Purpose y_<N>.act Strict typed classes for transform input. Mandatory leaves and leaves with defaults are available as non-optional values. y_<N>_loose.act Loose typed classes for transform output. All fields except list keys are optional, so a transform can emit only the values it intends to change. y_<N>_oper.act Loose typed classes that include config-false state and generated subscription paths for the layer. base_<N>.act Base classes implemented by transforms, together with helpers such as o_root() for creating output for the next layer. t_<N>.act Runtime glue that connects transform implementations, target links, and the transform tree.

Transform implementations normally import base_<N> and subclass one of its generated base classes. The strict and loose y_ types are then encountered through the transform input and output objects. The t_<N> module is an implementation detail of the generated application and does not normally need to be imported directly.

For example, a mandatory asn leaf has different types in the input and output modules:

# y_0: transform input
asn: u64

# y_0_loose: transform output
asn: ?u64

The loose output is intentional. Transform output is partial and is merged with output from other transforms further down the stack.

items.title: Device modules
items.text:
Each device type produces three modules in src/<project>/devices/:

Module Purpose <device>.act Typed, config-true device classes used to construct configuration, for example with root(), create(...), and to_gdata(). <device>_oper.act Typed operational view that includes config-false state and generated subscription paths. <device>_schema.act The compiled YANG schema represented as Acton data. The config module imports it, and the runtime uses it when validating and serializing data.

The schema module is not a backup copy of the generated API. Separating the large schema data from the typed config classes keeps the generated modules manageable while preserving the schema needed at runtime.

The operational module is used when reading state or declaring telemetry subscriptions. See Subscriptions for the generated subscription API.

items.title: Application wiring
items.text: Compilation also creates the modules that assemble the application. The generated sysspec.act imports each layer and device module, builds the layer stack, and registers the config and operational schemas for every device type. The generated device_types.act provides the device type registry. Unlike the other generated files, it is only created when missing so a project can extend the registry with device types supplied by other packages.
